name: Intel 4004 CPU
summary: The Intel 4004 put a complete four-bit computer processor on one silicon chip, first designed for Busicom calculators and then sold to other equipment makers.
description: The Intel 4004 four-bit silicon-gate CPU, including early development iterations and later merchant offers as separately scoped events; peripheral chips remained part of MCS-4. Intel museum history credits Hoff and Mazor with developing the architecture and Faggin with Shima with implementing the design.
tier_reason: The scoped record is a particular configuration, local witness, trial or material application. Dependence across fields or generations on THIS referent is not established; do not inherit the importance of its broader missing family.
why: The Japanese calculator maker Busicom commissioned a chip set from Intel, and Intel proposed a general programmable processor to reduce the number of custom chips.

market.note: The documented product sale or offer establishes market applicability, without establishing first commercial availability of the complete configuration.

evidence.supports: The 4004 was offered as part of the in-stock MCS-4 family.

date.label: January 1971
date.basis: Participant account describes working wafer run in January and subsequent correction of minor bugs.

events.statement: A 4004 silicon run worked in January 1971; subsequent tests found and corrected minor errors.
events.scope: Early Intel 4004 working silicon with minor bugs, not the later corrected production mask
events.caveats: The participants describe a working early iteration; this event is not a claim that it was the final mask sold in November.

evidence.locator: IEEE Micro December 1996, printed pp. 16–17/PDF pp. 7–8, The 4004 comes to life
evidence.supports: Project participants describe early 4004 chips that worked in January 1971, bug fixes and fully functional iteration in March.

date.label: 15 November 1971
date.basis: Intel advertisement reports the MCS-4 family in stock on this day.

events.statement: On 15 November 1971 Intel advertised the MCS-4 family, including the 4004, as in stock for its merchant market.
events.scope: Intel 4004 CPU offered as part of the MCS-4 family; the advertisement does not identify a mask or physical iteration.
events.market: Merchant component sales outside exclusive desktop-calculator applications
events.caveats: The first day of merchant sales and possible earlier private merchant offers are unresolved. Earlier availability to Busicom under its contract is a different market scope.

evidence.locator: Reproduced 15 November 1971 Intel advertisement, final two paragraphs
evidence.supports: Names the 4004 and says the MCS-4 family was in stock at Intel offices in the United States, Europe and Japan.
Busicom contract initially exclusive; by May 1971 Intel acquired rights to sell for uses except desktop calculators.

date.label: April 1969
date.basis: The 4004 team’s retrospective dates Intel’s agreement to develop calculator chips for the Japanese firm to April 1969.

events.statement: Intel agreed to develop calculator chips for the Busicom-associated Japanese firm.
events.scope: Initial calculator-chip development arrangement, before the eventual 4004 implementation.
events.caveats: The account does not supply a contract price here; the initial agreement is not a sale to the general market.

evidence.supports: The authors describe an April 1969 agreement to develop calculator chips for the Japanese firm.
Intel agreed to develop chips for the Busicom-associated firm.

earliest_record.rationale: Earliest defensible dated record of this scoped referent in the retained evidence; later community entry is recorded separately. Participant account describes working wafer run in January and subsequent correction of minor bugs. The participants describe a working early iteration; this event is not a claim that it was the final mask sold in November. This is the earliest supported record currently established here, not certification of absolute priority.

community_entry.community: Prospective Intel merchant-market buyers outside desktop calculators
community_entry.rationale: The 15 November 1971 advertisement says the Intel MCS-4 family, including the 4004, was in stock at named offices.
community_entry.caveats: This is a dated offer and available-by evidence, not proof of the first possible sale or first Busicom delivery. Named offices do not prove equal stock or actual transactions in each country.

caveats: The early working iteration and merchant-offered devices are not asserted to have identical masks. First merchant or Busicom availability and first sale remain unknown.

links.statement: Faggin carried silicon-gate expertise to Intel and added logic-process features used to implement the 4004.
links.scope: Fairchild to Intel, 1968–71; process knowledge, with Faggin joining Intel in 1970.
links.alternatives: AL1 CPU slices and MP944 multi-chip processing were contemporary alternatives.
links.caveats: The multiplexer circuit itself was not a CPU component; the transmitted contribution was process/design capability. Architecture had distinct contributors.
links.timing: 1968 deployment and 1970 transfer precede the 1971 CPU.

evidence.supports: Intel adoption, Faggin transfer and buried-contact enhancement.

links.statement: Federico Faggin recalled using a 1702 EPROM program with a 4004-controlled production tester.
links.scope: One Intel production-tester configuration; not a claim that EPROM was necessary for all 4004 systems.
links.alternatives: Other 4004 applications could use other memory devices and arrangements.
links.caveats: The account is retrospective and does not establish a customer sale or all masks and versions of the tester.
links.timing: The internal prototype context is separate from either component’s selected merchant-availability anchor.

evidence.supports: Faggin recalls using 1702 EPROM program storage with a 4004-controlled production tester.

links.statement: The 4004 is a MOS integrated implementation; its transistor function belongs to the insulated-gate MOS architecture.
links.scope: Only the identified configurations and source-described contribution.
links.alternatives: No unique historical route or universal necessity asserted.
links.caveats: Device-class function, not use of Atalla and Kahng’s physical prototype or a demonstrated personal transmission route.
links.timing: The relation concerns the scoped events and functions; no transmission inferred from chart placement.

evidence.locator: 1971 milestone, MOS LSI and silicon-gate implementation narrative
evidence.supports: The 4004 is a MOS integrated implementation; its transistor function belongs to the insulated-gate MOS architecture.

unresolved.note: Working early 4004 silicon is documented separately; no unique invention date is inferred from it.

evidence.locator: IEEE Micro December 1996, printed pp. 16–17/PDF pp. 7–8, The 4004 comes to life
evidence.supports: Project participants describe early 4004 chips that worked in January 1971, bug fixes and fully functional iteration in March.

unresolved.note: The 15 November advertisement proves an in-stock offer by that date, but not the first day of merchant availability. Earlier contractual Busicom commerce is also unresolved.

evidence.locator: Reproduced 15 November 1971 Intel advertisement, final two paragraphs
evidence.supports: Names the 4004 and says the MCS-4 family was in stock at Intel offices in the United States, Europe and Japan.
Busicom contract initially exclusive; by May 1971 Intel acquired rights to sell for uses except desktop calculators.

research.note: Four-bit CPU identity merges architecture and product contexts; exact development and market stages remain separate. Contributor attributions are preserved from the removed dated assertion and its elec-chm-4004-cpu and elec-chm-silicon-gate evidence.
